item.title: Meet Nkechi Okenwa, the Engineer Helping More Nigerian Women Break Into Renewable Energy
item.dc:creator: Bird
item.description:
In Nigeria, where renewable energy is increasingly becoming a necessity rather than an alternative, women like Nkechi Okenwa are working to bridge both gaps at once, bringing clean energy solutions to underserved communities while creating pathways for more women to enter the sector.

The post Meet Nkechi Okenwa, the Engineer Helping More Nigerian Women Break Into Renewable Energy appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Tokunbo Adegoju during an interview with bird story agency at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

Nkechi Okenwa walked into her office, moving instinctively toward the window and pulled the blinds open. Outside, the city was already in motion: cars weaving through traffic, traders arranging their stalls, generators humming faintly in the distance. She paused for a moment and smiled quietly to herself. For Nkechi, energy had never simply been about electricity. It was about movement, opportunity, and the power to transform lives.

Long before she stepped into a university lecture hall, Nkechi said, she had been fascinated by the way a single switch could completely change the atmosphere of a home. Growing up in Nigeria, she watched how electricity brought light into dark rooms and how access to power allowed communities and businesses to function.

“As a teenager choosing the course of study, I had to take on electrical electronics engineering as a course,” she recalls. “Though I knew it was a male-dominated call, because I never saw any female studying that course… that’s actually how this whole journey started.”

When she finally entered university, the reality of that gender gap became impossible to ignore. In a lecture hall of more than 220 engineering students, only 12 were women — barely five percent of the class. The imbalance was intimidating, but it also planted the seed for a bigger mission.

Tokunbo Adegoju during her radio show at the Eko FM in LTV premises 1, lateef Jakande way , Agidingbi ikeja, Lagos, July 9, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

“I said there has to be a way to, you know, get women inclusive.”

“I understand the challenges that come with a female being in this male-dominated industry, but when I look at myself and I can remember how I was able to go through, the challenges, my persistence, and all of that, I told myself it’s possible that so many other women too have aspirations to make a difference in their world and can also do this, so it made me start thinking of starting this organisation.”

Years later, that determination evolved into two major ventures. Today, Nkechi serves as the CEO of Energy Excell Systems and Solutions and is also the founder of the Women in Energy and Economic Sustainability Initiative (WEESI), which is dedicated to integrating women into every level of the renewable energy sector.

Tokunbo Adegoju repairing a car at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

Her professional journey did not begin with entrepreneurship. After graduating, she started as a technical staff member at an IT company where she worked with power systems and tools like AutoCAD. Through workshops, conferences, and industry engagements, she became increasingly exposed to the renewable energy sector at a time when Nigeria was slowly beginning to embrace alternative energy solutions.

She later transitioned into a sales executive role before eventually building her own solar installation company.

Established in 2013, Energy Excell Systems and Solutions Limited operates as an indigenous Nigerian renewable energy social enterprise and Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) company. But beyond simply installing solar panels, the company focused heavily on what Nkechi describes as “productive use” energy.

The company provided homes, small businesses, and farming communities with energy-efficient appliances such as solar-powered rice mills, cassava graters, and grinders: tools capable of directly improving livelihoods and local economies.

Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

As her business expanded, Nkechi noticed another problem that extended far beyond electricity access. Women remained largely absent from conversations around energy solutions, despite being among the most affected by energy poverty within communities.

“I looked at women, and I found that most challenges in the community that we face, we face them as men and women, but I find that women sometimes are not really included in solving these challenges, so I told myself I have to find a way to get women to across all levels.”

That realisation led to the creation of WEESI in 2020. The initiative was designed to create pathways for women and girls across the energy value chain, from rural communities at the bottom of the energy pyramid to leadership spaces within the sector.

The organisation strategically tailored its programs across different age groups. For girls and young women between the ages of 12 and 26, WEESI organised STEM essay competitions, mentorship programmes, and scholarship opportunities aimed at nurturing early interest in renewable energy and engineering.

Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

At the grassroots level, the initiative focused heavily on economic empowerment. Rural women, community entrepreneurs, and internally displaced persons (IDPs) received technical training in solar photovoltaic installation and maintenance while also learning sustainable clean cooking practices.

“We have carried out programs and trainings with women in the rural areas, ranging from telling them how to turn the waste in the community into energy, like making and manufacturing charcoal briquettes with the waste in the community. For example, a woman that threshes rice and has a heap of rice husk doesn’t even know what to do with it. Now, can decarbonise this rice husk into charcoal and make briquettes with them, and make profitable money from it?”

For many women, the impact of WEESI became life-changing.

Tokunbo Adegoju and fellow mechanics discussing with each other at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

Among them was Anita Manuel, an entrepreneur and contractor working with an oil and gas firm. Anita first encountered WEESI during its launch and immediately felt drawn to the organisation’s mission.

“What drew me to the initiative is that their objectives aligned with my values and goals too, and I just wanted to expand my business,” Manuel said.

Through the training, Manuel learned practical skills in solar panel installation, energy auditing, and technical troubleshooting. More importantly, she began to see how her background in project management and civil works could fit into the renewable energy sector.

One moment, however, remained unforgettable.

The first time she participated in a successful solar installation that powered an entire building and activated a freezer became a defining experience. For Manuel, it was proof that the technical knowledge she had gained was not theoretical; it was transformative.

Mechanics at the Automedics workshop repairing a car in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

For Nkechi, her growing influence in the renewable energy space was a quieter battle many women in STEM continue to face: self-doubt and institutional bias.

Even after earning her engineering degree, she often questioned whether people would truly trust her expertise in such a male-dominated field.

“My fears were, are you sure that I’m going to do it right? Are you sure people are going to listen to me because I’m a woman?”

Those fears were reinforced repeatedly in professional spaces. Clients frequently walked into her office searching for a male engineer, assuming she could not possibly hold the technical expertise herself.

Tokunbo Adegoju engaging with new students on their first day at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

“So many times, a man will walk into my office and want to make inquiries about our products and services, and asking me, ‘Where is the technician here? Where’s the engineer here?’”

“And I said, ‘Sir, talk to me, I am the engineer.’ Even the way he approaches me and talks to me shows that he’s still not confident.”

Instead of retreating, Nkechi leaned deeper into her work, allowing technical excellence to speak louder than assumptions.

“With time, as I kept confronting my fears, as I kept going head-on with it, I, at least, have overcome those fears to a reasonable extent,” she says.

While stories like Nkechi’s reflect progress, Nigeria’s renewable energy sector still faces major structural challenges. High installation costs continue to limit adoption rates, while policy inconsistencies and poor-quality installations by untrained technicians have created skepticism around solar technology.

One of the mechanics at the Automedics workshop repairing a car in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), nearly 600 million people across Africa still live without access to electricity, with sub-Saharan Africa accounting for the largest share of the global electricity access gap. It notes that expanding access to electricity in Africa will require rapid investment in mini-grids, solar systems, and decentralised renewable energy solutions, especially in rural communities where grid expansion remains limited.

For electrical and renewable energy engineer Eng. Ale Oluwafeyisayo Joy, Nigeria still lags behind countries such as Kenya and South Africa in renewable energy adoption.

“In Nigeria, I would say that we’re not yet in full adoption,” Joy assesses. “And that’s due to a couple of factors, as compared to countries like Kenya and South Africa that have been able to get it right in certain structural development, fat running policies, and also clear pathways and finances.”

Still, she believes the future of renewable energy in Nigeria is inevitable.

“Solar is not an option; it’s actually a necessity. I believe it being that way means that in the nearest future, in the coming months and years from now, it will be something that we get very competitive in the market expansion.”

Tokunbo Adegoju repairing a car at the Automedics workshop in Illepeju, Lagos, July 10, 2026. Photo: Dorcas Bello, bird story agency

For Nkechi, that future is about more than market growth or technology adoption. It is about changing who gets to participate in building that future.

It is about ensuring that the next generation of girls entering engineering classrooms never feels out of place. It is about creating an industry where women no longer need to prove they belong before they are heard.

And somewhere inside her office each morning, as she stands by the window watching the world come alive, Nkechi continues building exactly that kind of future; one powered not only by energy but by inclusion, persistence, and possibility.

***
Story Credit: Simpa Samson for Bird Story Agency

If there’s one thing Cynthia Erivo has mastered, it’s the art of keeping us guessing. Whether she’s embracing full-throttle red carpet glamour or experimenting with more directional silhouettes, the British actress rarely plays it safe. And judging by her latest appearances, she’s showing no signs of slowing down.

For the Prima Facie premiere at the BFI London Film Festival, Cynthia delivered a welcome dose of sunshine in a custom canary-yellow Prada gown. The bias-cut satin skimmed her figure beautifully, falling into a sweeping train, while oversized black grosgrain bows at the shoulders added a graphic contrast to the otherwise minimalist silhouette.

@jasonbolden 

And she’s just as convincing in something that’s more casual but still directional. Case in point: the tan leather Proenza Schouler Fall 2026 co-ord she wore in New York. With its structured double-breasted jacket, relaxed trousers and chunky platform shoes, the look could easily have felt overwhelming. Instead, Cynthia made a compelling case for exaggerated proportions, proving that a neutral palette doesn’t have to mean playing it safe.

Her final appearance at New York Comic Con, where she joined the cast of Children of Blood and Bone in another Proenza Schouler Fall 2026 creation also designed by new Proenza Schouler Creative Director Rachel Scott (also of Diotima). This time, she opted for a navy printed dress featuring sculptural draping, an asymmetric silhouette and dramatic fringed detailing. The silver grommets along the hem introduced an unexpected industrial edge, while glittering blue heels and statement jewellery completed the look.

Three months, four pool parties, two Saturday night parties and one unforgettable task Smirnoff Ice has left its mark on the BBNaija house. The season was a full celebration of what Bolder with Ice stands for: self expression without limits. Inside the house, that meant housemates showing different sides of themselves depending on their mood, and the energy of the moment, and Smirnoff Ice was right there for every one of them.


The pool parties set the tone early. With music playing and a cold Smirnoff Ice in hand, the housemates danced, had fun in the pool and laughed their way through every moment. Some stayed in the pool, others at the edge, while some didn’t stop dancing the whole time. That’s kind of the beauty of Bolder with Ice, there really isn’t a “right” way to experience it. You just show up, find your pace, and take it all in. Whether you’re there to lose yourself in the music or just relax with a cold drink, the whole point is simply being there and enjoying the moment.


The Saturday night parties carried that same energy into the evening. The housemates stepped out in outfits they picked for themselves, danced to the music and enjoyed the night with their friends in the house. Every look and every dance move was theirs, which is exactly the kind of individuality the brand was built to celebrate.

Then there was the Smirnoff Ice task: Bolder With Ice Challenge, where the house got to play, create and compete. Broken telephone, the Ice Throne styling challenge, the memory game, Shadow Partner and the painting round gave the housemates room to show their humour, their style, their focus and their creativity. Team Original and Team Double Black went head to head, but the real win was the laughter and the personality that came out of every round.


That is what made the Smirnoff Ice season special. Across the pool parties, the Saturday night parties and the task, there was always room for every mood. The loud one, the quiet one, the stylish one, the playful one, the competitive one, all of them had a place and all of them had a good time. Smirnoff Ice did not ask the housemates to be anything other than themselves, and that is exactly the idea behind Bolder with Ice.

As the season comes to an end, the memories will stay: the music, the pool, the dance floor, the games and the friendships built along the way. Thanks to every single housemate who brought their own kind of bold to the house, and a massive thank you to everyone who tuned in, laughed, and celebrated with us all season long.

Until the next season, stay bold, stay chilled, and stay you.

item.title: Dayo Akinbode: What Planting an Okra Tree Taught Me About Life and Kindness
item.dc:creator: Dayo Akinbode
item.description:
Sometimes, the most beautiful things in our lives begin with a seed we never intended to plant. As I stood in my garden admiring the green okro pods ready for harvest, I smiled. As I looked at the beautiful green pods, my thoughts travelled back several months to a seemingly insignificant encounter with my neighbour, […]

item.content:encoded:
Dayo Akinbode narrates what planting an okra tree taught her about kindness. Credit: Dayo Akinbode

Sometimes, the most beautiful things in our lives begin with a seed we never intended to plant. As I stood in my garden admiring the green okro pods ready for harvest, I smiled. As I looked at the beautiful green pods, my thoughts travelled back several months to a seemingly insignificant encounter with my neighbour, which is the story behind my okra harvest.

Earlier in the year, my neighbour offered me okro seeds to plant, but I declined them. I was not interested in planting okro, and I simply did not see the need. My neighbour, however, went ahead and planted the seeds in my garden. Imagine! So the seeds I declined were now nestled in the soil of my own garden, beginning a journey I had not planned for them.

Those tiny seeds would eventually become flourishing plants that would supply my kitchen with fresh okro for months. I certainly did not imagine that I would one day stand admiring my harvest and reflecting on the deeper meaning of what had happened.

Life has a way of surprising us like that.

As the weeks passed, the plants grew, and I began to appreciate the beauty of watching nature at work. What begins as a tiny, almost insignificant seed gradually transforms into a living plant, reaching towards the light and preparing to produce something useful. And boy, there is something fascinating about harvesting food from your own garden.

Whenever the flowers on the okra plants came – the yellow, hibiscus-like flowers – I knew harvest time was around the corner. Those bright splashes of yellow against the green leaves became a familiar and welcome sight. Each time I saw them, I felt a little excitement, knowing that fresh okro pods would soon appear, and then be ready for harvest.

The bright yellow, hibiscus-like flowers of the okro plant, signalling that harvest time is approaching. Credit: Dayo Akinbode

The process of planting okra is not so different to our lives, too. We plant seeds when we start a business, pursue a dream, learn a new skill, nurture a friendship or encourage someone who is struggling. Sometimes, we see results quickly. At other times, progress appears slow, and we begin to wonder whether anything is happening at all. The absence of an immediate harvest does not necessarily mean that nothing is happening. Sometimes, growth is taking place quietly, beyond what we can see. And occasionally, there are little signs along the way that remind us to keep going, just as those yellow flowers reminded me that my okro harvest was approaching.

As I reflected on this, I found myself thinking again about my neighbour and her simple act of kindness. She offered me something useful, and when I declined, she still found a way to share her gift with me. I wonder whether she imagined how much I would appreciate those plants months later. Whatever her motivation, her act taught me to be kind to people even when they can’t see or appreciate the value. We have all been there, one way or the other.

This also made me wonder how many opportunities we dismiss because we cannot immediately see their value. A friend shares an idea we are not ready to embrace. Someone offers help we think we do not need. A person introduces us to an opportunity that seems unimportant at the time. We wave such opportunities away and move on, unaware of what might have grown from them. Of course, not every offer should be accepted, and we must exercise our judgement. We can learn to remain open to possibilities. Perhaps we can then enjoy the benefits of a decision we did not make ourselves, just as I am with the okra.

Today, I am grateful for my okro harvest, and for my neighbour and her kindness. I am equally grateful for the reminder the okro growth has given me. Kindness can grow, patience can yield rewards, and an unexpected beginning can become a beautiful harvest.

So, as I admire the fruits of my neighbour’s simple gesture, I find myself asking two questions: What seeds are we planting in the lives of others? And what beautiful harvest are we enjoying today because someone once planted a seed for us?

item.content:encoded:
Samuel Animashaun Perry (Broda Shaggi) explains the stray bullet incident behind his months-long hiatus in a new video.

If you are a fan of Broda Shaggi‘s skits, his music, or even just his lively presence on your timelines, you must have noticed that the popular entertainer and actor has been noticeably absent from social media over the past few months. Samuel Animashaun Perry has now officially returned, bringing along a deeply moving mini-documentary that breaks his silence and reveals the terrifying life-threatening ordeal behind his sudden hiatus.

The multi-AMVCA winner revealed that his unexpected break was caused by a horrific incident where he was struck by a stray bullet while returning from a shoot. Recounting the frightening moment, Broda Shaggi shared,”We were done shooting and were on our way when we got stuck in a holdup. Suddenly, I heard a loud bang and everywhere went silent. I could see people talking, but I couldn’t hear anything. Then I touched my hip and saw blood. That was when it dawned on me that I had been hit by a stray bullet.”

Broda Shaggi in an eccentric futuristic costume for one of his signature video skits.

The incident led to an emergency hospital admission, extensive medical procedures, and an intensive period of physical rehabilitation. For a performer whose entire craft relies on boundless physical energy, comedy, and stage presence, being bedridden and unable to move presented immense physical and emotional hurdles. In the video, he candidly reflects on the overwhelming fear of losing his mobility and the uncertainty of how he would continue doing what he loves.

Tracing his road from severe setback to resurgence, the documentary shows his gradual process of learning to walk again, moving from complete immobility to crutches and eventually regaining his strength. Now stepping back in front of the camera on his own terms, Broda Shaggi is turning what could have been a tragic end into a triumphant second chapter, ready to reconnect with his fans and dive back into his creative work.

If these photos of Osas Ighodaro have you staring at your screen a little longer than usual, we completely understand. Because how do you look at a dress this beautiful and simply scroll past? The colours, the design, the way it sits on her body! There’s so much to admire, and we’re right there with you.

The Nigerian-American actor, host and producer has given us many reasons to love her fashion choices over the years, but this particular look has us especially curious about how it was made. Dressed in a gorgeous blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee, Osas looks like she stepped straight out of an art exhibition. And once you hear the inspiration behind the dress, you might appreciate it even more.

Actor and host Osas Ighodaro wearing a blue mosaic gown crafted from hand-painted mother-of-pearl by House of Marvee.

Here’s where it gets interesting. House of Marvee drew inspiration from thermal mapping, using different shades of blue to follow the natural curves of the body. The floor-length gown features hand-painted mother-of-pearl details, creating a mosaic effect that moves between deep ocean blues and brighter turquoise tones. Look closely, and you’ll notice how the colours and textures work together across the fabric.

Osas Ighodaro posing in an asymmetrical one-shoulder blue mosaic dress featuring hand-painted mother-of-pearl tiles by House of Marvee.

We also love how the one-shoulder design gives the dress room to shine. One arm is covered in a long sleeve, while the other shoulder is left bare, creating a lovely contrast. Osas keeps her accessories simple with gold hoop earrings, allowing the beautiful details of the gown to remain the focus.

Osas Ighodaro posing in a House of Marvee hand-painted mother-of-pearl blue gown with gold hoop earrings and a finge

And can we talk about her beauty look for a second? The retro finger waves, warm-toned makeup and gold hoop earrings complement those gorgeous shades of blue beautifully. From the hand-painted details to the way the gown follows her silhouette, House of Marvee has given us a dress we’d happily spend a few more minutes admiring.

item.content:encoded:
Toyin Abraham’s directorial comedy drama Oversabi Aunty is now streaming on Netflix and Kava.

Your next movie night could take you from a hilarious Nollywood comedy to a fantasy world full of adventure, or straight into a crime story that keeps you guessing. With several Nollywood films and series now available to stream, there’s plenty to add to your watchlist before October wraps up. Whether you’re in the mood for a box-office hit you missed at the cinema or a moving coming-of-age story, these are the titles worth making time for.

Oversabi Aunty (Streaming on Kava TV and Netflix)

Toyin Abraham’s record-breaking directorial debut follows Toun, a self-righteous church usher whose overzealous obsession with fixing everyone else’s morals turns her home and family life into a chaotic battlefield. Her relentless meddling reaches its breaking point during a disastrous family introduction, forcing her to confront the emotional fallout and damage she has caused her loved ones. Directed, written, and produced by Toyin Abraham alongside FilmOne Studios, the witty dramedy features an ensemble cast including Toyin Abraham, Mike Ezuruonye, Jemima Osunde, Tana Adelana, Efe Irele, Enioluwa Adeoluwa, and Queen Nwokoye.

Colours of Fire (Streaming on Netflix)

Niyi Akinmolayan’s epic fantasy film takes viewers into an ancient world where the fabric-weaving Blue Tribe and the mysterious Red Tribe maintain a bitter, generational conflict. When a warrior named Akinbode is sent to eliminate a beast terrorising his people, his unexpected encounter with Moremi—the daughter of the Red Tribe’s queen—ignites a forbidden romance that challenges inherited stories and threatens to unravel their entire society.

Directed and written by Niyi Akinmolayan, with production credits from Anthill Studios, FilmOne Studios, and Imuetinyan Productions, the visually rich film stars Uzor Arukwe, Osas Ighodaro, Mercy Aigbe, Gabriel Afolayan, Femi Branch, and Ibrahim Chatta.

Ordinary People (Streaming on Netflix)

Moses Inwang’s crime thriller series dives deep into the gritty, interconnected lives of characters navigating power, ambition, and survival across the streets of Lagos and beyond. The story exposes how everyday decisions spiral into high-stakes consequences when ordinary individuals find themselves caught in webbed conflicts and dangerous secrets.

Created, directed, and written by Moses Inwang, the eight-episode production features a powerhouse cast starring Ramsey Nouah, Adunni Ade, Chidi Mokeme, Sharon Ooja, Michelle Dede, Shawn Faqua, Lasisi Elenu, Uche Montana, and Jackie Appiah.

Where Is Mr Right? (Streaming on Prime Video)

Tunde Olaoye’s romantic drama follows Bunmi, an event planner facing immense societal and familial pressure to get married before crossing an arbitrary age milestone. Her determined quest to locate an ideal partner spirals into a series of comedic missteps, unexpected heartbreaks, and lessons on patience and self-discovery.

Directed by Tunde Olaoye and written by Funke Akindele, who also serves as executive producer, the film brings together a stellar cast including Omowunmi Dada, Blossom Chukwujekwu, Bisola Aiyeola, and Funke Akindele.

The Almajiri (Streaming on Prime Video)

Ibrahim Jammal’s coming-of-age drama centers on Rabiu, an exceptionally gifted young boy in the ancient city of Kano who defies poverty and traditional dogma in pursuit of formal education. Raised under the Almajiri system, Rabiu secretly receives lessons from a supportive teacher, dreaming of becoming a tech engineer while navigating the strict resistance of his religious instructor.

Directed by Ibrahim Jammal and Obinna Ohazulike, written by Kynene Oma, and produced by Steve Gukas, Dotun Olakunri, and Kester Nsirim, the film stars breakout child actor Ahmed Isa alongside Yakubu Mohammed, Jamila Ibrahim, Sani Mu’azu, Musa Mohammed, and Ijapari Ben–Hirki.

item.content:encoded:
Nigerian Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Dara Ojo was stuck at home in China, like everyone else in the world. He had recently picked up photography, and that allowed him to explore and pay close attention to his immediate surroundings.

One day, he started paying closer attention to the tiny creatures around him and was amazed by what he was seeing. There were colours, patterns, behaviours and details that he had never noticed before. It felt like discovering an entirely different world that had been right in front of me all along.

Dara self-taught himself macro photography, and the seemingly small curiosity during the pandemic has grown into a journey of documenting biodiversity across Nigeria, Canada, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador and beyond. His work has travelled globally and has been featured in major international publications. Dara has photographed over 40 types of spiders, 50 species of moths, 30 species of butterflies, more than 20 dragonflies, and at least 70 damselflies.

There are many photographers in Nigeria, but seeing that macro photography is not often explored by Nigerians, we sat down for a brief conversation with Dara, where he shared what inspired his form of photography, what documenting biodiversity in different environments has taught him about nature and his forthcoming first photography book, Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem.

Leafhopper infected by Metarhizium Fungus. Photo by Dara Ojo.

Hey Dara, how are you feeling?

I feel good. I feel blessed. Thank you for having me.

What do you think inspired or attracted you to macro photography?

Growing up in Nigeria, I never really thought of insects as something beautiful or worth photographing. Like many people, I saw them as creatures you either avoided or tried to get rid of. But once I started looking at them through my camera, my perspective completely changed.

What fascinated me most wasn’t just how they looked, but how they lived. I started asking questions. Why does this spider behave this way? How does that tiny insect survive? What role does it play in nature?

The more I discovered, the more curious I became. Six years later, that curiosity has taken me from photographing tiny creatures around my neighbourhood in China to exploring rainforests and other ecosystems across different continents. And the interesting thing is that I still experience that same excitement whenever I discover something new. I don’t think that feeling will ever go away.

Bumblebee by macro photographer, Dara Ojo.

The excitement. How can you describe it? When taking a shot, what do you feel that you hope people also feel when they encounter the photo?

Wonder. That’s probably the best word to describe it.

Sometimes I’m photographing a creature, and I genuinely cannot believe what I’m looking at. It might be the incredible colours of a jumping spider, the delicate patterns on a moth’s wings, or an insect doing something I’ve never witnessed before. There have been moments when I’ve found myself laughing out of excitement because nature has surprised me again.

That’s the feeling I want people to experience when they see my photographs.

I know some people might initially feel uncomfortable looking at a spider or another creature they’re afraid of, and that’s perfectly understandable. But if they can look at that photograph for a few more seconds and begin to notice something fascinating rather than frightening, then I feel I’ve accomplished something.

I’m not necessarily trying to make everyone love insects or spiders. I just want people to become curious enough to see them differently. Because sometimes, curiosity is all it takes to change how we treat the natural world.

Silk Worm Moth by Nigerian macro photographer, Dara Ojo

As someone who has photographed in different parts of the world, how has documenting biodiversity in different environments shaped your perspective on nature? 

One of the biggest things I’ve learned is that extraordinary biodiversity isn’t limited to the places we traditionally associate with wildlife photography. I’ve photographed in China, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador, Canada and Nigeria, and every environment has taught me something different.

In the rainforests of Costa Rica and Ecuador, I’ve encountered creatures with some of the most remarkable adaptations I’ve ever seen. In Canada, I’ve spent countless hours photographing tiny wildlife in places people walk past every day. Even a small garden can be home to an incredible diversity of species.

But returning to photograph in Nigeria was particularly meaningful to me.

Treehopper by Nigerian macro photographer, Dara Ojo.

What do you think people might be surprised to learn about Nigeria’s insect life and biodiversity?

I think many Nigerians would be surprised by just how much biodiversity exists in our own country. Nigeria has an extraordinary range of habitats, from tropical rainforests in the south to savannas in the north, supporting an incredible variety of life.

When people think about African wildlife, the conversation often centres on lions, elephants and other large animals. But there’s an entire world of smaller creatures that rarely receive the same attention.

During my time photographing in Nigeria, I encountered some fascinating species, including the praying mantis that eventually became the cover of my book.

And that’s something I find particularly special. After travelling across different continents and photographing so many remarkable creatures, the photograph chosen to represent my first book came from Nigeria. It reminds me that we don’t always have to travel halfway around the world to discover something extraordinary. Sometimes, we simply need to pay closer attention to what’s around us.

Mantis, by Nigerian macro photographer Dara Ojo.

Let’s talk about the book

Yes! Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. My first photography book.

Tell us about it and what you hope people take away from the book?

This book means a great deal to me because it represents six years of curiosity, exploration and learning. It brings together around 120 of my photographs from different parts of the world, alongside stories about the creatures I’ve encountered and the important roles they play in nature.

I wanted to create something that people could enjoy visually, but that would also encourage them to think differently about creatures they might normally overlook.

These tiny animals are doing some of the most important work on our planet. They pollinate plants, recycle nutrients, help control populations of other organisms and provide food for countless species. Without them, the ecosystems we depend on would look very different. Yet many are misunderstood, feared or simply ignored. What makes the book particularly meaningful to me is that it also tells a personal story. It follows my journey through different countries, including Nigeria, where I grew up, and Canada, where I now live.

I’m also incredibly honoured that Dr John Acorn, a respected Canadian entomologist and science communicator, wrote the foreword.

I hope someone picks up the book because they find the photographs interesting, but finishes it with a greater appreciation for the natural world, so that the next time they encounter a spider in their house or an unfamiliar insect in their garden, instead of immediately reaching for something to kill it, they’ll stop for a moment and take a closer look.

_

Dara Ojo’s Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem will be published on November 10, 2026, and will be available internationally. It will have public book launches in Edmonton on November 25 and Toronto on December 2, with additional events being explored for New York in March 2027 and Vancouver in April 2027. You can pre-order the book here.

item.content:encoded:
PPE Preparation in an Ebola Clinic. Generated Image.

Yesterday, October 20, 2026, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) announced the confirmation of the first Ebola virus disease case in Abuja. While the federal government and the NCDC have continued strengthening surveillance and response efforts to prevent its spread, it is important for Nigerian citizens to also stay alert, safe and take preventive measures.

According to the NCDC, “Ebola virus disease (EVD), also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever (EHF), is a severe disease of humans and other primates caused by an RNA virus of the family Filoviridae and genus Ebola virus. The disease has a high fatality rate, killing between 25%-90% of those infected. Research conducted in 2005 suggested fruit bats to be the likely reservoir due to their ability to spread the virus without being affected by it.

The largest outbreak to date took place in West Africa between March 2014 and June 2016, affecting Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Senegal, and Nigeria primarily. A total of 11,296 cases were recorded, including suspected and probable cases.”

The first-ever case of Ebola in Nigeria was confirmed in Lagos on 23 July 2014, and with its high fatality rate, citizens need to understand how to protect themselves before the government’s intervention.

According to the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Affairs, here are how you can protect yourself from Ebola virus disease:

Advice to Nigerians

Nigerians are advised to:

  • Practice good hand hygiene. Wash your hands regularly with soap under running water or use hand sanitisers when soap and water are not readily available.
  • Avoid physical contact with anyone who has symptoms of an infection with an unknown diagnosis.
  • Reduce the risk of wildlife-to-human transmission from contact with infected fruit bats or monkeys/apes and the consumption of raw meat. Animals should be handled with gloves and other appropriate protective clothing. Animal products should be thoroughly cooked before consumption.
  • Avoid direct contact with the blood, saliva, vomit, urine and other bodily fluids of suspected or confirmed EVD cases.
  • If you or someone you know (with a travel history to any country with Ebola cases) experiences symptoms of EVD enumerated above, call 6232 or your State Ministry of Health hotline IMMEDIATELY for guidance.
Advice to Healthcare Workers

Healthcare workers:

  • Are advised to maintain a high index of suspicion for EVD in their encounter with their patients
  • Ensure strict isolation of the patient(s).
  • Adhere strictly to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, including the use of appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) like face masks, hand gloves, appropriate gowns, safe sharps disposal and others.
  • Report suspected cases immediately to the NCDC or State Ministry of Health for appropriate response and management.
Advice to Travellers

Travellers are advised to:

  • Shelter-in-place to avoid further spread through shared transport systems (public or private) until health authorities reach out.
  • Await dedicated responders for assessment and possible transport to a designated treatment centre if required.

Ebola symptoms can vary, but the most commonly experienced symptoms at the beginning of the disease include a sudden onset of fever, intense weakness, muscle pain, headache, and a sore throat. As the disease progresses, other symptoms may develop, such as vomiting, diarrhea and jaundice (yellowness of the eyes).

In severe cases, individuals may experience uncontrolled bleeding from body orifices and dysfunction or failure of several organs, including the kidneys, liver, and central nervous system. This can lead to shock and, ultimately, death. In fatal cases, death often occurs between 8 and 9 days after the onset of symptoms.

Please contact NCDC for more enquiries or to report a suspected case on the toll-free number: 6232.

Stay safe, Nigerians.

item.content:encoded:
Sophia Chisom, Mike Afolarin, and Genoveva Umeh interpreting the rave glam dress code for Tele x Zikora.

A Nollywood premiere is always a good excuse to dress up, but when the dress code says “rave glam,” you know the red carpet is going to be anything but ordinary. That was the scene at the premiere of Tele x Zikora, where the cast and guests stepped out in bold colours, unexpected combinations and outfits that gave us plenty to look at.

Written, produced and directed by Adenike Adebayo–Esho, Tele x Zikora is a campus romance set at the fictional Lagos Metropolitan University. The film follows two young people from very different worlds whose paths cross, setting the stage for a love story. Ahead of its cinema release on 23 October 2026, the cast and crew gathered to celebrate, with the evening’s rave glam theme giving everyone room to experiment with their style.

Tele x Zikora writer, producer, and director Adenike Adebayo-Esho at the film premiere. Photo Credit: Adenike Adebayo-Esho/Instagram 

Sophia Chisom gave us a colour combination we wouldn’t have immediately put together, and somehow, it worked. She wore a royal blue longline coat over a matching top with a sharp white collar and cuffs, pairing both with a burnt-orange wrap mini skirt. An orange beret, star drop earrings and white knee-high boots completed her look.

Mike Afolarin took a different route with a cow-print shearling jacket, a black top and dark grey flared jeans featuring silver side-buckle details. He finished with a dark cap, keeping things casual while still having a little fun with the dress code.

Mike Afolarin at the Tele x Zikora premiere in a cow-print jacket and flare jeans. Photo Credit: Mike Afolarin/Instagram 

Then there was Genoveva Umeh in magenta and rose-pink sequins. Her dress featured structured shoulders and an asymmetrical skirt with long, shredded ribbons that moved as she walked. She paired it with deep pink tights and metallic heels, making a strong case for wearing pink from head to toe.

And those were only a few of the looks from the night. See how the cast and guests dressed for the Tele x Zikora premiere:
